title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) to measure whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) reduces unsafe intent→configuration proposals versus observing the identical initial LLM candidate without gating. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics, one sampled generation was reused for both arms per pair. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents in a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 200 shared initial candidates passed validation in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. Under the registered shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory contrast tests only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates; it does not measure guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt engineering, or multi‑sample/model variance. We present the preregistered design, execution accounting, artifact pointers, artifact‑grounded interpretation of this null result, and recommendations for follow‑up designs that avoid ceiling effects.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to convert high‑level operator intent into device configurations and maintenance workflows. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that operational safety depends heavily on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gating policies, and repair loops—rather than the model alone [1],[2]. Generate–validate–repair and guarded agent designs are repeatedly advocated as practical defenses, but reproducible paired evidence quantifying verifier/gate effects on the same sampled model candidate is limited. Research question: compared to observing a single LLM candidate without gating, does coupling that identical candidate with a deterministic validator and deterministic accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair attempt) reduce unsafe network‑change proposals on a fixed paired intent set? Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered paired design and frozen execution (autocand_A1_prereg_v1); (2) an autonomous run using gpt‑5‑mini and a Batfish‑style deterministic validator on n=200 paired intents with shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) confirmatory analysis (paired binary estimator), artifact‑grounded diagnostics, and a discussion of construct/internal/external validity with concrete recommendations.
sections.related_work: Recent work explores LLMs for NetOps and AIOps including intent‑based configuration, runbook generation, RCA, and limited remediation. Surveys and empirical reports document hallucination and safety risks and stress that external verifiers, retrieval anchoring and contractual checks are central to operational trustworthiness [1],[2]. Generate–validate–repair architectures appear across NetOps and adjacent domains (program repair, robotics) as practical defenses against unsafe outputs [3],[4]. Empirical DevOps/AIOps reports show retrieval and command‑safety checkers can reduce unsafe command emissions in specific pipelines but do not guarantee zero hallucination; these works call for validator‑coupled benchmarks and reproducible paired comparisons [5],[6]. Our experiment implements a preregistered paired test under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure validator/gate effects on identical initial candidates, addressing this methodological gap.
sections.methodology: Preregistration: study id autocand_A1_prereg_v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 archived). Execution adapters and tooling: model = gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); orchestration adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Generation semantics (critical): shared_initial_candidate — exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and reused for both baseline and guarded arms per paired intent; therefore the confirmatory estimand evaluates only validator/repair/gate effects on that same first‑pass candidate. Sampling and tasks: preregistered task_count = 200 paired intents (selection deterministic per adapter index rule). Tasks exercise workflows (VLAN migrations, failover, MTU upgrades, composed maintenance) with explicit sequencing and protected‑interface constraints. Intervention: baseline = observe initial candidate; guarded = observe same initial candidate then run deterministic validation, deterministic gate (accept/reject), and at most one automated repair attempt if validator reports violations (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1). Primary metric and estimand: binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or workflow/policy violation reported by the validator after candidate stabilization; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Analysis (frozen): paired binary analysis executor (exact McNemar‑equivalent implemented by registered executor), two‑sided alpha=0.05; primary missingness policy = complete_pair_primary; paired bootstrap percentile CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed=1729). Implementation artifacts and authoritative manifests (archived) contain per‑episode traces, validator traces, and execution accounting.
sections.results: Execution accounting: planned_episode_count = 400 (200 pairs), completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per pair). Confirmatory contingency counts (guarded × baseline): n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (artifact: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Primary estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0. Exact two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. Paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). Repair activity: repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes (no automated repairs executed). Validator final_state reported valid = true for every paired final configuration (validator traces archived per episode; representative examples available). Latency: median end‑to‑end time dominated by the shared initial generation; guarded overhead was negligible because no repairs triggered. Missingness and exclusions: no pairs excluded; missingness summary artifact records complete_pairs = 200.
sections.discussion: Interpretation of the degenerate null result: under the registered shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory estimator strictly measures whether the deterministic validator/gate (and its at‑most‑one repair attempt) would change acceptance decisions for an identical sampled candidate. Observing n11=200 (all candidates valid) means the guarded pipeline produced no different outcomes because every shared initial candidate already satisfied validator rules. Plausible contributors to this ceiling effect include: (1) the deterministic synthetic task generator and chosen prompt/template produced high baseline solvability for gpt‑5‑mini on these tasks; (2) shared_initial_candidate semantics prevented guarded‑conditioned regeneration that could produce different guarded candidates in other experimental regimes; (3) validator rule classes closely mirror task constraints so valid generator outputs align with validator expectations. Archival evidence: deterministic validator enforces sequencing/workflow constraints, per‑interface field constraints (VLAN/MTU change rules), protected‑interface protections, and group‑level active constraints; these behaviors are recorded in per‑episode validator_trace.validation_before/after fields. Implications for design: to reveal measurable verifier value researchers should (i) include adversarial/OOD items or a task bank with nontrivial baseline unsafe rates, (ii) consider independent guarded‑conditioned regeneration or multiple independent samples per condition rather than shared_initial_candidate semantics, (iii) evaluate multiple models/temperatures, and (iv) instrument rollout‑centric metrics (rollbackability, canary safety) in richer emulation.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment (n=200 pairs) under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing an LLM‑alone observation to the same initial candidate after a deterministic verifier+gate and bounded repair. Every sampled initial candidate passed the deterministic validator and the guarded pipeline changed no outcomes (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]). This artifact‑grounded null result is specific to the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), synthetic task bank and deterministic selection, the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and the shared_initial_candidate semantics; it does not contradict prior reports that verifiers help under alternative experimental regimes (e.g., guarded‑conditioned regeneration, adversarial inputs). We provide archived artifacts and a pragmatic roadmap for follow‑up experiments that are more likely to detect verifier benefits.

limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or prompt engineering.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions, vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank reporting: the archived task_manifest.jsonl is authoritative for per‑label counts. The manifest is dominated by tasks labeled 'very_hard' with a minority labeled 'extreme'; exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest (see execution/task_manifest.jsonl in the artifact bundle).
